title: Scout 80 / 800
verdict: A tractor company was told to build something to replace the horse, and ten years later it was selling V8 wagons with bucket seats. Same 100-inch wheelbase, same honest steel box, and more rust than any seller will admit to.

paragraphs: International Harvester had built farm machinery and trucks for half a century when, in the late 1950s, it decided to build a rival to the Jeep CJ, then in its [[jeep/cj-5|CJ-5]] era. Chief designer Ted Ornas later said the brief from the engineering manager was to "design something to replace the horse." The result, the Scout 80, went on sale in late 1960 as a 1961 model and was built in Fort Wayne, Indiana. Autotrader Classics puts first-year sales at about 28,000. Not bad for a tractor company's first go at a small 4x4.

story.heading: A HORSE REPLACEMENT FROM FORT WAYNE
paragraphs: According to Silodrome, the early proposals looked a lot like the Jeep and the [[land-rover/series|Series Land Rover]]. Ornas's curvier sketches, drawn for a plastic body, won management over. Plastic turned out to be too expensive, so the Scout was built in steel. The first clay model was made in June 1959 and approved that November. For an engine, IH took its 304 cubic-inch V8 and used one bank of it: a 152 cubic-inch slant-four, rated at 93 horsepower.

The first Scout was basic. It had a fold-down windshield, vacuum wipers mounted on top of the glass, and, until early 1962, side windows that slid out rather than wound down. It sat on a 100-inch wheelbase with Dana 27 axles front and rear, both offset to the passenger side, and a Dana 18 transfer case behind a three-speed. You could buy it as a pickup, an open roadster or a TravelTop wagon, in two- or four-wheel drive. Sports Car Market says the four-wheel-drive TravelTop was the one buyers wanted most.

story.heading: THE 80 GROWS UP
paragraphs: By 1964 IH had built more than 100,000 Scouts. It marked the occasion with the Red Carpet edition, about 3,000 trucks in white with red interiors. The Scout 800 arrived for 1965 with a fixed windshield, wipers moved to the bottom of the glass, an aluminum grille, bucket seats, better gauges and a better heater. It was the start of the Scout's slow move from work truck toward family wagon. Japan's [[land-cruiser/fj40|FJ40]] was a contemporary rival.

The engines grew too. A turbocharged 152 made 111 horsepower. The 196 cubic-inch four, half of IH's 392 V8, arrived in 1966 with the same 111 horsepower and better fuel economy. An AMC-built 232 inline-six followed, and in 1967 the Scout got its first V8, IH's own 266. The 1966 Sportop had a raked fiberglass roof and a nicer interior, and the rare factory Campermobile came with fold-out bunks. Both were early signs of the lifestyle SUV, years before anyone called it that.

story.heading: 800A AND 800B: THE LAST OF THE ORIGINALS
paragraphs: The 800A arrived in November 1968 with a three-piece grille and black headlight bezels. The other half of the 304 V8 was now in the options list, and running gear was heavier. Wikipedia lists a Dana 44 rear axle and a quieter Dana 20 transfer case for the 800A, while Autotrader Classics dates both changes to 1967, so check the truck rather than the paperwork. The 800A also brought the Aristocrat, the dressiest of the original-body Scouts, in blue and silver with a chrome roof rack.

The 800B, built from August 1970 to March 1971, was almost identical except for chrome headlight bezels. It came with a Comanche package, with its own paint and decals, and a SnoStar snowplow package offered only with the six. Production of the [[scout/scout-ii|Scout II]] began in April 1971. Hagerty sums up the original run well: the Scout beat Ford's Bronco to market as a more practical alternative to the Jeep CJ, and it was among the early SUV pioneers.

story.heading: OWNING ONE NOW
paragraphs: Hagerty credits early Scouts with a reputation for durable drivetrains, which it puts down to IH's tractor-building background. The same sources agree that the bodies are the problem. Silodrome warns that trucks driven on salted roads can end up "looking like a colander", and the catalogues of IH Parts America and Super Scout Specialists, full of replacement floors, rockers and patch panels, tell the same story. The good news is that the parts exist. Autotrader Classics notes that large panels such as fenders are not reproduced, but small steel is.

Prices have moved a long way. Sports Car Market recalled that its author bought a 1967 Scout 800 V8 TravelTop for $800 in 2003. In mid-2024, Autotrader Classics advised budgeting at least $40,000 for a good one and warned that anything under $15,000 is a major project. Volkswagen Group now owns the Scout name, and its [[scout/scout-motors|Scout Motors]] revival is building a factory in South Carolina. Its website's coordinates, 41°03'N 85°04'W, point straight back to Fort Wayne.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE SCOUT THAT WENT TO PATAGONIA
callout.title: Pato, the factory camper, and the Pan-American Highway
paragraphs: IH offered an experimental factory camper body for the Scout 80. It cost $960 installed as a stripped shell or $1,850 as a deluxe unit. Few were built, and Wikipedia calls them rare today.

One of them went a very long way. According to the man who uploaded the photo below to Wikimedia Commons, his father and a college roommate were given a 1963 or 1964 Scout 80 Camper by International for a drive from Denver to Patagonia on the Pan-American Highway. In return they supplied photos from the trip for IH's print advertising. They named the Scout 'Pato', and it was sold in Santiago, Chile, at the end of the trip. It might still be there.

engineering_intro: The Scout is a steel body on a ladder frame with a 100-inch wheelbase, leaf springs at all four corners and drum brakes all round. Four-wheel-drive trucks use Dana axles, closed-knuckle at the front, with a two-lever Dana transfer case and hubs that stick out past the hub caps. Power steering and power brakes were options, and Silodrome says a truck with both is the better buy. The engines all came from one family: the fours are halves of IH's V8s.

engineering.note: 154 in long overall. The same basic body was used from 1961 to 1971.
Forward-shackle front springs. IH Parts America calls the ride on stock geometry "a bit choppy."

engineering.note: Closed-knuckle front axle, both axles offset to the passenger side. Power-Lok limited-slip was optional.
Twin-stick shifter on the 80 and 800. The Dana 20 is quieter.
The 152 is half a 304 V8, and the 196 is half a 392.
Power brakes were optional. Front disc conversions are a common upgrade.

buying_checks.head: Rust is the whole story
buying_checks.body: Autotrader Classics says to check the rockers, the windshield and side-window frames, and the lower corners of the removable top. Silodrome adds the spring mounts, the insides of the fenders and the welds, and warns that rust starts on the inside and works out, so bubbling paint is a bad sign. The fact that IH Parts America sells front and rear floors, inner and outer rockers, and fuel-tank compartment panels tells you where else to look.

buying_checks.head: Count the big panels
buying_checks.body: Small steel parts are widely reproduced, but Autotrader Classics notes that no one makes large panels such as fenders. A truck that needs fenders is a much bigger job than one that only needs floors.

buying_checks.head: Is it really a 4x4?
buying_checks.body: Scouts were sold in two-wheel drive too. Autotrader's quick test: if the hub sticks out through the hub cap, it's a four-wheel-drive truck. Then look for the twin transfer-case levers.

buying_checks.head: Confirm the year and the engine
buying_checks.body: Binder Planet hosts Jim Allen's list of starting and ending serial numbers for the 80, 800, 800A and 800B, compiled from IHC records, so you can date the truck and confirm which model it is. On an IH V8, Super Scout Specialists says the displacement is stamped on a domino-sized flat spot on the right side of the block, toward the front and just below the head. Engine swaps are common.

buying_checks.head: Listen to the driveline
buying_checks.body: Autotrader Classics advises checking the axles and transfer case for wear. A transfer case that pops out of gear needs to come out for a rebuild, according to an IH Parts America moderator. On the front axle, look for worn knuckle wipers and sloppy kingpins.

buying_checks.head: Power options matter
buying_checks.body: Silodrome says Scouts with both power steering and power brakes are the better buy, because without them steering and braking take real effort. Autotrader Classics calls the four-wheel drums archaic and says a four-cylinder probably won't reach 75 mph.

buying_checks.head: Ask what's been changed
buying_checks.body: Suspension and other modifications are common, so ask the seller for details. That includes lifts, shackle swaps, disc conversions and engine transplants. A good conversion can be a plus. An undocumented one is a list of questions.

repairs.title: Floor pan and rocker replacement
repairs.symptoms: Soft or holed floors under the mats, rockers bubbling at the bottom of the doors, and daylight around the fuel-tank compartment. Silodrome warns that rust usually starts inside and works out.
repairs.fix: Strip the interior and measure everything before cutting. Cut out the rotten metal and fit replacement front floor halves (sold by side), the rear floor, and inner and outer rockers as needed, with the front floor X-brace if it's gone. Weld the panels in, seam-seal and paint. If the body is lifted or off, replace the body-mount bushings while you're there.
repairs.tools: MIG welder · cutoff wheel and spot-weld drill · clamps and self-tapping screws for fitting · seam sealer and weld-through primer.

repairs.title: Swap the vacuum wipers for an electric kit (800 series)
repairs.symptoms: The original vacuum wipers on an 800 are dead, sluggish or simply not worth rebuilding.
repairs.fix: IH Parts America's bolt-in kit mounts below the windshield where the vacuum motors were. One two-speed, self-parking 12-volt motor drives both arms through a linkage, and the kit is designed to clear the original gauges, radio, speaker and glove box. Remove the vacuum motors and linkage, fit the brackets and bushings, mount the motor, run power through the new switch, and fit the arms and blades. The optional deluxe switch adds intermittent and washer functions. The Scout 80's top-mounted wipers are a different design, so check fitment before ordering.
repairs.tools: Basic hand tools · drill · wiring crimpers · test light.

repairs.title: Front knuckle seals and kingpin bearings (closed-knuckle Dana)
repairs.cost: $19.95 per IHPA seal kit (two per axle); kingpin bearings extra
repairs.symptoms: Grease weeping from the knuckle balls, torn wipers, and play in the knuckle when you rock the wheel top to bottom. One IHPA forum owner described his 1968 800 this way: "the wipers for the knuckles are shot and the king pin bearings are worn out."
repairs.fix: With the axle supported, pull the wheel, hub, spindle and axle shaft. Inspect the axle U-joint while it's out. Remove the knuckle seal retainer and the kingpin caps, then replace the kingpin bearings and races and set preload with shims. Fit the new seals and wipers, reassemble, and repack the wheel bearings. The IHPA seal kit fits the small eight-bolt knuckles, not the large 12-bolt ones, and you need two kits per axle. We couldn't source the kingpin preload figure, so use the IH shop manual.
repairs.tools: Floor jack and stands · hub/bearing nut socket · seal driver · torque wrench · inch-pound scale for preload · wheel-bearing grease.

repairs.title: Transfer case pops out of gear: Dana 20 rebuild
repairs.cost: Overhaul kit plus labor, or buy a rebuilt case
repairs.symptoms: The transfer case jumps out of 2-High or won't fully engage 4-High. On a 1967 800, an IHPA forum member found the shift-cover opening was too small for the levers to travel fully, so check that before you strip the case.
repairs.fix: Drain the oil first. Support the engine and transmission with a second jack or blocks, and disconnect both prop shafts at the output flanges. The case weighs about 70 lb. An IHPA moderator recommends a full rebuild with a master overhaul kit rather than band-aid fixes. The service manual lists bent forks, a bad spring or bearings as possible causes. Refill with SAE 90 GL-1 mineral oil, or straight 50-weight motor oil as a substitute, and not 80W-90 GL-5. Early Scout 80s and 800s use the Dana 18, so order the right kit.
repairs.tools: Transmission jack or a second floor jack · puller · snap-ring pliers · seal drivers · gasket scraper.

repairs.title: Front disc brake conversion
repairs.cost: Kit plus a day of labor
repairs.symptoms: Four-wheel drums that fade, pull or simply don't stop a V8 Scout on modern roads.
repairs.fix: The CPT kit sold by IH Parts America for 1966–71 800s with Dana 27 or 30 front axles includes new hubs, 11 3/4-inch vented rotors, caliper brackets, calipers, pads, stainless hoses, a disc/drum master cylinder, a proportioning valve and a pushrod. It reuses your wheel bearings, and the knuckles must be ground for caliper clearance. It replaces the dual-circuit master cylinder found on 1967 and later 800s. Single-circuit trucks and Scout 80s need extra hard lines. Some stock 15- and 16-inch drum-brake wheels won't clear the calipers. Bleed the whole system afterwards.
repairs.tools: Die grinder · flare-nut wrenches · bearing packer · brake bleeder · tube flaring tool for 80s and single-circuit trucks.

repairs.title: Springs, shackles and bushings (fix the sag and the ride)
repairs.symptoms: A tired stance, clunks from worn spring eyes and shackles, and the choppy ride of forward-shackle front springs.
repairs.fix: Replace the springs, shackles, bushings, U-bolts and shocks as a set. IH Parts America says its CPT system for 1961–71 Scouts nets 1 to 3 inches of lift, about 2 inches on most trucks. It includes heavy-duty springs, 4-inch shackles, 1/2-inch U-bolts, 2-degree caster shims, Bilstein shocks and an extended rear brake hose. You may need to notch around the front driveshaft and transmission crossmember and enlarge the U-bolt plate holes. For a better ride, CPT's reverse-shackle kit moves the front shackle. It needs welding and drilling through the frame, and a longer-travel front driveshaft is recommended.
repairs.tools: Jacks and stands · penetrating oil and heat for seized bolts · torque wrench · drill (and welder for a reverse-shackle kit).

repairs.title: Points to electronic ignition
repairs.cost: Module or distributor plus an hour
repairs.symptoms: Hard starting, a misfire that comes and goes, and points that keep closing up. Silodrome lists electronic ignition among the sensible upgrades.
repairs.fix: First identify your distributor, because Super Scout Specialists sells different Pertronix Ignitor modules for the Holley and Delco distributors used on the fours. Pull the cap and rotor, remove the points and condenser, fit the Ignitor to the breaker plate, and wire it to the coil as the instructions show. Set the timing with a light. A complete HFI distributor is the alternative if the shaft or bushings are worn.

baseline_service.intro: Treat any early Scout as a 50-plus-year-old machine whose fluids could be any age. Baseline everything, then inspect the front knuckles, brakes and steering before trusting it on the trail. Factory capacities for the 80 and 800 weren't available in sources we could verify, so check the IH shop manual or owner's manual for those. The one firm rule from IH specialists: keep GL-5 gear oil out of the transfer case.

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: We couldn't find a forum consensus for a bone-stock 80 or 800. The best data point comes from IH Parts America, which says "a 31" tire should fit fine" with its CPT spring system. That system adds 1 to 3 inches, about 2 on most trucks, and IHPA's own 800B runs 31x10.50 Duratracs on Scout II rally wheels. IHPA also notes that the front tires can hit the rear of the front wheel well, which its reverse-shackle kit addresses by moving the axle forward. So on stock springs, stay close to stock size. With fresh lift springs, 31s are the realistic ceiling.

faq.q: What's the difference between the 80, 800, 800A and 800B?
faq.a: The 80 (1961–65) has the fold-down windshield, top-mounted vacuum wipers and the 152 four. The 800 (1965–68) got a fixed windshield, bucket seats, better heating and gauges, plus the 196 four, 232 six and 266 V8. The 800A (late 1968–70) added the 304 V8, a three-piece grille and black headlight bezels. The 800B (August 1970 to March 1971) is the same truck with chrome bezels.

faq.q: Which engine should I look for?
faq.a: The 152 four makes 93 hp, and Autotrader Classics warns that a four-cylinder probably won't hit 75 mph. The 196 four makes 111 hp, the same as the 152 turbo, with better economy. For trail use and highway speed most people want the 266 or 304 V8, but they sit in a heavier nose. Check the block stamping to confirm what's actually fitted.

faq.q: Is the four-cylinder really half a V8?
faq.a: Yes. The 152 is one bank of IH's 304 V8, and the 196 is half of the 392 V8. That's why the engines share so many parts, and why the fours lean over in the engine bay.

faq.q: What oil goes in the transfer case?
faq.a: IH specialists on the IH Parts America forum recommend SAE 90 GL-1 mineral oil, or straight 50-weight motor oil as a substitute, filled to the bottom of the filler hole with the truck level. One moderator estimated the capacity at about 2.5 to 3 quarts. Don't use 80W-90 GL-5.

faq.q: What gear oil for a Power-Lok or Trac-Lok rear axle?
faq.a: Use 80W-90 with a limited-slip additive, according to IHPA forum regulars. One owner found Mobil 1 gear oil made his Power-Lok chatter, while Red Line and Royal Purple worked.
No. The Scout was sold in two- and four-wheel drive from the start, and Wikipedia says four-wheel drive became standard by 1968. To check a truck, see whether the hub protrudes through the hub cap.

faq.q: How do I date my Scout and confirm the model?
faq.a: Use the serial number. Binder Planet hosts a list of starting and ending serial numbers and VINs for the 80, 800, 800A and 800B, plus the special models. Jim Allen, author of the International Scout Encyclopedia, compiled it from IHC records and microfiche. The data plate is on the driver's side of the cowl.

faq.q: What is an early Scout worth?
faq.a: In mid-2024 Autotrader Classics advised budgeting at least $40,000 for a good example. It said a semi-decent one starts around $25,000 and anything under $15,000 is a major project. Restored trucks have sold for far more, including $33,000 for a Scout 80 at Barrett-Jackson in 2014 and a $114,900 asking price for a frame-off 800A.

Yes, and more than for many trucks this age. IH Parts America and Super Scout Specialists list floors, rockers, patch panels, brakes, axle seals, transfer-case kits and wiring. Silodrome notes that engine and transmission parts are widely available. The gap is large panels: Autotrader Classics says no one reproduces fenders.

faq.q: Can an early Scout be made into a usable daily or trail truck?
faq.a: Yes, if you upgrade the right things together. Common jobs are a front disc conversion, a power-brake booster, a power-steering conversion (CPT makes one for 800A and 800B with the IH V8), new springs and shackles, and electronic ignition. Silodrome's advice is that any power upgrade should come with better brakes, a stronger transmission and better suspension.
